{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Chevalley–Shephard–Todd theorem''' in [[invariant theory]] of [[finite group]]s states that the [[ring of invariants]] of a finite group [[group action|acting]] on a [[complex number|complex]] [[vector space]] is a [[polynomial ring]] if and only if the group is [[generating set of a group|generated]] by [[pseudoreflection]]s. In the case of [[subgroup]]s of the complex [[general linear group]] the theorem was first [[mathematical proof|proved]] by {{harvs|txt=yes|first=G. C. |last=Shephard |author1-link=Geoffrey Colin Shephard|first2=J. A.|last2= Todd|author2-link=J. A. Todd|year=1954}} who gave a case-by-case proof. {{harvs|txt=yes|authorlink=Claude Chevalley|first=Claude |last=Chevalley|year=1955}} soon afterwards gave a uniform proof. It has been extended to finite [[linear group]]s over an arbitrary [[field (mathematics)|field]] in the non-modular case by [[Jean-Pierre Serre]].

== Statement of the theorem ==

Let ''V'' be a [[dimension (vector space)|finite-dimensional]] vector space over a field ''K'' and let ''G'' be a finite subgroup of the general linear group ''GL''(''V''). An element ''s'' of  ''GL''(''V'') is called a '''pseudoreflection''' if it fixes a codimension 1 [[linear subspace|subspace]] of ''V'' and is not the [[identity transformation]] ''I'', or equivalently, if the [[kernel (linear operator)|kernel]] Ker(''s'' − ''I'') has [[codimension]] one in ''V''. Assume that the [[order (group theory)|order]] of ''G'' is [[coprime]] to the [[characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]] of ''K'' (the so-called non-modular case). Then the following properties are equivalent:<ref>See, e.g.: Bourbaki, ''Lie'', chap. V, §5, nº5, theorem 4 for equivalence of (A), (B) and (C); page 26 of [http://www.home.uni-osnabrueck.de/wbruns/brunsw/Mel65.pdf] for equivalence of (A) and (B{{prime}}); pages 6&ndash;18 of [http://www.ltcc.ac.uk/courses/Invariant%20Theory%20of%20Finite%20Groups/InvariantTheory-week3.pdf] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140729204329/http://www.ltcc.ac.uk/courses/Invariant%20Theory%20of%20Finite%20Groups/InvariantTheory-week3.pdf |date=2014-07-29 }} for equivalence of (C) and (C{{prime}}) [https://mathoverflow.net/q/32456] for a proof of (B{{prime}})⇒(A).</ref>

* (A) The group ''G'' is generated by pseudoreflections.
* (B) The algebra of invariants ''K''[''V'']<sup>''G''</sup> is a (free) [[polynomial algebra]].
* (B') The algebra of invariants ''K''[''V'']<sup>''G''</sup> is a [[regular ring]].
* (C) The algebra ''K''[''V''] is a [[free module]] over ''K''[''V'']<sup>''G''</sup>.
* (C') The algebra ''K''[''V''] is a [[projective module]] over ''K''[''V'']<sup>''G''</sup>.

In the case when ''K'' is the field '''C''' of complex numbers, the first condition is usually stated as "''G'' is a [[complex reflection group]]". Shephard and Todd derived a full classification of such groups.

== Examples ==

* Let ''V'' be one-dimensional. Then any finite group faithfully acting on ''V'' is a subgroup of the multiplicative group of the field ''K'', and hence a [[cyclic group]]. It follows that ''G'' consists of [[roots of unity]] of order dividing ''n'', where ''n'' is its order, so ''G'' is generated by pseudoreflections. In this case, ''K''[''V''] = ''K''[''x''] is the polynomial ring in one variable and the algebra of invariants of ''G'' is the subalgebra generated by ''x''<sup>''n''</sup>, hence it is a polynomial algebra.
* Let ''V'' = ''K''<sup>''n''</sup> be the standard ''n''-dimensional vector space and ''G'' be the [[symmetric group]] ''S''<sub>''n''</sub> acting by permutations of the elements of the standard [[basis (linear algebra)|basis]]. The symmetric group is generated by [[transposition (mathematics)|transposition]]s (''ij''), which act by reflections on ''V''. On the other hand, by the main theorem of [[symmetric function]]s, the algebra of invariants is the polynomial algebra generated by the [[elementary symmetric function]]s ''e''<sub>1</sub>, ..., ''e<sub>n</sub>''.
* Let ''V'' = ''K''<sup>2</sup> and ''G'' be the cyclic group of order 2 acting by ±''I''. In this case, ''G'' is not generated by pseudoreflections, since the nonidentity element ''s'' of ''G'' acts without fixed points, so that dim Ker(''s'' − ''I'') = 0. On the other hand, the algebra of invariants is the subalgebra of ''K''[''V''] = ''K''[''x'', ''y''] generated by the homogeneous elements ''x''<sup>2</sup>, ''xy'', and ''y''<sup>2</sup> of degree 2. This subalgebra is not a polynomial algebra because of the relation ''x''<sup>2</sup>''y''<sup>2</sup> = (''xy'')<sup>2</sup>.

==Generalizations==
{{harvtxt|Broer|2007}} gave an extension of the Chevalley–Shephard–Todd theorem to positive characteristic.

There has been much work on the question of when a reductive algebraic group acting on a vector
space has a polynomial ring of invariants. In the case when the algebraic group is simple all cases when the invariant ring is polynomial have been classified by {{harvtxt|Schwarz|1978}}

In general, the ring of invariants of a finite group acting linearly on a complex vector space is [[Cohen-Macaulay]], so it is a finite-rank free module over a polynomial subring.
